iodine deficiency and iodine excess are both harmful to the health of the mother and fetus.
the iodine status in the mothers is not related to the neonatal thyroid function, and iodine supplementation in mothers does not seem to be necessary.

the use of antepartum thyroid function testing in all women with a personal history of autoimmune thyroid disease (AITD) is not recommended, but should be considered in those with positive thyroid peroxidase (TPOAb) antibodies, and in women with AITD who are at high risk of fetal loss.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the iodine status of the mothers is not a predictor of the iodine status in their newborns and that the iodine levels in newborns were not a predictor of neonatal TSH values.
the use of antepartum and postpartum iodine-containing disinfectants is a risk factor for iodine excess and transient hyperthyrotropeinemia in newborns in a mildly iodindeficient region.
we have shown that iodine excess in mothers and newborns is a common phenomenon, and it may lead to transient hyperthyrotropicemia and increases in screening costs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of iodized salt is not adequate for preventing iodine deficiency.
iodine excess in newborns leads to transient hyperthyrotropeinemia, which increases the recall rate in screening programs for congenital hypothyrodism.
iodine excess in neonates is a common problem and is associated with high recall rates in mildly iodine-deficiency areas.
